Automating trial curation

An agentic pipeline for ~2,000 free-text cancer trials
Junran Cao  ·  Hartwig Medical Foundation  ·  30 July 2026
Background

Improving clinical trial recommendations on somatic NGS reports

Oncologists need clear, accurate and current information to interpret genomic findings and weigh what they mean for patient care. How therapeutic information is included and presented still varies widely between laboratories and reporting systems.

The variation

Reporting practice differs between laboratories

Pendlebury et al. surveyed laboratories across Australia and New Zealand and found substantial variation in reporting practice.

Almost a quarter of participating laboratories did not include therapeutic options in their NGS reports at all.

The standards

Best practice has been proposed

AMP–CAP and ESMO have both proposed standardised NGS reporting.

The aim is a better clinician experience — results that are easier to comprehend and to read.

What it demands

Six things a report must keep current

Rapidly changing evidence, regulatory approvals, reimbursement arrangements, clinical context and reporting responsibilities — plus the systems to maintain all of it over time.

Clinical trial matching is one part of that reporting problem. This talk describes the challenges Hartwig met building tools to streamline it.
The problem

The scale and the rate of change require automation

Hartwig curates the trial universe for Australia and New Zealand so that a patient's molecular profile can be matched against the trials open to them. Two properties of that universe determine how it has to be built.

Scale

2,041 open oncology trials

Across two registries: 5,284 trial arms and 17,830 distinct combinations of eligibility requirements.

The eligibility of each arm, and the drugs it administers, are described in free text.

Continuous change

Records are added, amended and closed

Between our 25 July snapshot and the 29 July download — four days — 71 trials had entered the universe and 32 had left it.

A curated resource therefore has a short shelf life.

At this scale and this rate of change, both ingestion and curation have to be automated and repeatable, so that the resource can be rebuilt on a schedule.
The problem

From free text to a structured, matchable resource

The key sections of each trial arrive as free text. We transform them into a structured resource file with controlled vocabulary for the downstream matching engine. It has three sections.

Section 1

Basic details

Recruitment status, phase, sponsor, locations — the basic info fields, carried through deterministically.

Section 2

Eligibility

Who qualifies — cancer type, gene alterations, biomarkers, prior therapy — as structured logic in controlled vocabulary (OncoTree, finding-model syntax).

Section 3

Drug utility

The interventional drugs — canonical identity, class, targets, and TGA / PBS approval status.

All three sections must be machine-interpretable: every value in controlled vocabulary where one exists, and every value traceable back to the source text it came from.
The problem

Transforming free text into structured vocabulary is difficult

Eligibility criteria are written for human readers. The structure a matching engine needs is present in the text but not marked, and has to be recovered before any value can be mapped to vocabulary. Four recurring difficulties:

Difficulty 1

Alternatives are not delimited

“with MYCN amplification, or focal high level MYC or MYCL amplification” NCT04221035 states three alternatives, of which a patient needs one. Nothing in the text marks where one ends and the next begins.

Difficulty 2

Requirements combine

A cancer type, an alteration and a prior-therapy condition usually apply together, and different arms of the same trial combine them differently. Each valid combination is a separate way to qualify.

Difficulty 3

Exclusions have a scope

An exclusion may apply to the whole trial or to one arm of it. “not eligible for the surgical cohort” constrains that cohort only, and applying it trial-wide would exclude eligible patients.

Difficulty 4

Terminology varies

The same disease appears as an abbreviation, a full name, or a list of histologies. Across the trial universe there are 4,971 distinct ways of writing a cancer type, and each has to resolve to the correct code.

The problem

Where our first attempt fell short

Version 1 was a linear chain of one-shot LLM calls over the eligibility section, corrected manually afterwards. Five problems motivated the rewrite.

Problem 1

No automated verification

A linear chain of one-shot LLM calls requires a human reviewer. Virtually impossible to manually detect all errors across ~2,000 trials.

Problem 2

No combinations of eligibility criteria

Cancer type and gene alterations were treated as independent criteria, so cancer × gene combinations needed manual overwriting.

Problem 3

No external web search for drug enrichment

Drug annotations — drug class, target–mechanism, and TGA / PBS status — cannot be filled from the protocol text alone.

Problem 4

Reliance on handcrafted mapping files

No reliable means of transforming input text into our controlled vocabulary without manually created mapping files.

Problem 5

Read only the eligibility section

Eligibility-relevant detail also appears in the title, description, conditions and arm text, which version 1 did not read.

Part 1 · trial ingestion and updating

Where the trials come from

Two registries, downloaded in full on every run and filtered locally to the trials we curate.

ClinicalTrials.gov — 1,525 trials

Retrieved by API

A paged search with the filters applied at the registry.

ANZCTR — 516 trials

Retrieved as a whole-registry export

ANZCTR has no search API, so we download the entire registry (91 MB) and apply the same filters locally. 777 trials matched; 516 had a drug intervention.

a priority list that overrides the filters A published list of Australian trials must always be included. It widens the registry search and exempts those trials from the drug-intervention filter — 30 non-drug trials were kept on that basis.
versioned inputs Each download becomes the current version and the previous one is archived, so a run can be reproduced against the exact input it read.
Part 1 · trial ingestion and updating

Keeping the resource up to date

The pipeline is designed to be re-run regularly. Each cycle compares the fresh download against what is already curated, and only work that has not been done before consumes any LLM calls.

1 · RE-DOWNLOAD BOTH REGISTRIES IN FULL  —  apply the filters  →  the current set of trials we keep
▾
2 · each trial falls into one of three cases. “New” here means new to the kept set, which is not the same as newly registered
▾
in the download, not yet curated
New → curate it
Either a new registration, or an existing trial whose record changed so that it now matches the filters. Within it, only drugs absent from the reference are researched.
71 trials · 25 → 29 July
in the download, already curated
Unchanged → skip it
The stored answer is returned against a fingerprint of the request, so no LLM call is made.
~1,960 trials, near-instant
curated, absent from the download
Retired → moved aside
Its recruitment status changed — completed, withdrawn or terminated — so it no longer matches. Its rows are moved to a holding area, and restored intact if it returns.
32 trials · 25 → 29 July
3 · the common case, from this week. NCT06652438 is a phase 3 AML trial first submitted on 2 October 2024, with no Australian site. Its record was updated on 27 July 2026 and posted on 29 July, adding 10 Australian sites — so it began matching the location filter and entered the kept set that day. An international trial opening Australian sites is precisely the change a regular refresh exists to catch.
Part 2 · trial curation · the shared pattern

Both curation paths use the same pattern: a doer and its reviewers

Every LLM step on the eligibility path and the drug utility path has the same shape: one agent writes the whole answer, focused reviewers judge it against the source, and any objection sends it back to be rewritten.

✗ a reviewer objects  →  back to the doer, with the critique
doer

Reads the source and writes the whole answer in one pass.

→answer
reviewer panel

Several focused agents, each judging one aspect, in parallel.

→verdict
decision

All clear → done.
An objection → round again, up to 6 times.

why checking works better than writing Producing a correct answer is a search problem; checking a proposed one is closer to a look-up. Think of a mathematical proof: finding it can take years, while checking a written proof is a careful read. So we spend the most capable effort on the doer, and can afford several cheaper reviewers to catch its mistakes.
the extraction panel — five reviewers, one aspect each

A narrow check is far more reliable than one agent judging everything at once.

cancer typemolecularstructureprior therapydrug

A reviewer can object but never rewrites — so every value in the output was written by the doer and then checked.

Part 2 · trial curation · dividing the work

What code computes, and what an LLM must judge

Anything with one correct value that can be looked up is resolved by code, and is never asked of an LLM.

Computed programmatically

Facts with one right answer

  • drug identifiers and class codes, from a drug reference
  • whether a code or an expression is valid at all
  • which trials are new and which have gone
  • every join, de-duplication and the final file

The LLM supplies a drug's name; code turns that name into its identifier. A wrong identifier would corrupt every join that depends on it.

Judged by an LLM

Reading, interpretation, search

  • what a sentence actually requires of a patient
  • which alternatives are real, and which are examples
  • which drug an arm is testing, and which is supportive
  • finding a drug's mechanism and approval status on the web
  • whether a mapping is faithful to the source text

Each of these requires reading the source and forming a judgement about it.

Each side is given only the work it is reliable at: the LLM reads and interprets; the code computes, validates and joins.
Part 2 · trial curation · verifying correctness

Spot checks — every individual value, as it is produced

Each value is checked twice before it is stored: once for faithfulness to the source, and once for form.

Is it faithful to the source — checked by an LLM reviewer
  • Does every quoted span really appear in the source
  • Is the cancer type the tumour under study
  • Is each molecular value in the right column
  • Are only required and excluded prior therapies treated as constraints
  • Is the row structure and per-arm scope correct
  • Is the vocabulary code faithful, at the right level of detail
  • For a drug: the right ingredients, a plausible mechanism and class, sourced TGA / PBS entries, and its role in the arm
Is it well-formed — checked by code
  • Is the cancer code valid, and the alteration expression syntactically valid
  • Is anything self-contradictory — the same term required and excluded
  • Is a code duplicated, or a broad type ANDed with its own subtype
  • Is the OR / AND precedence unambiguous
  • Did the drug identifier, class and ATC code come from a lookup
  • Are exact-duplicate and merely re-ordered rows removed
Part 2 · trial curation · verifying correctness

Overall checks — the finished cycle, before it is trusted

Spot checks cannot detect a cycle that curated only half the universe and still produced a plausible-looking file. Ten deterministic gates examine the finished state on disk — no LLM, no network.

integrityfail

Every eligibility, drug and role row points at an arm that exists.

empty outputfail

Every arm producing no eligibility carries a reason. An unexplained empty is a possible miss.

retirementfail

A retired trial is gone from every table.

exportfail

Exactly the expected columns; no curated trial missing without a reason.

nothing lostfail

Reference data never shrank, and after = before − retired + newly curated holds exactly.

download sanityfail

Retirement was not skipped by its own safety guard.

completenessfail

Every trial in the fresh universe is in the store.

universe swingwarn

The kept universe changed by less than 10% against the previous cycle.

output validatorwarn

An independent pass re-checks the finished file and reports how many trials are clean.

waived findingswarn

Known, accepted findings stay visible as a warning, so a gate fails on new problems rather than on a standing backlog. Each waiver is code, reviewed in git, and names its follow-up.

how a failure surfaces Any FAIL makes the run exit non-zero so the scheduler sees it, and writes STATUS.json for a monitor to poll. WARN means look, but the data is usable.
a durable record per cycle One Markdown run report: the universe, which trial ids were retired, restored and newly curated, a before–after delta for every table, and each gate's verdict.
Part 2 · trial curation · the checks in practice

Three real corrections, one from each layer of checking

Caught by an LLM reviewer

An example became a requirement

The source excluded EGFR mutations, then added “gene mutations that do not routinely use immunotherapy (e.g. ALK fusion)”. The doer made the example mandatory:

NOT(EGFR) AND Fusion[ALK]

The reviewer objected: the phrase is open-ended and ALK is only an illustration — requiring it narrows the trial to patients it never specified. Corrected to drop the term.

Caught by a deterministic check

A mapping that contradicted itself

A mapping came back with the same cancer code both required and excluded in one expression:

… PCM … AND NOT(PCM)

No patient can satisfy that, so the row would silently match nobody. The validator rejects X AND NOT(X) outright — it needs no judgement, so it never gets one wrong. The usual cause: two cohorts' requirements folded into one row.

Caught across all trials

The same disease, two different codes

Mapped trial by trial, equivalent phrasings drift apart. A run-wide pass compares every value across all trials: code normalises the equivalent ones, and an LLM adjudicates genuine conflicts.

“Astrocytoma”: DIFG → ASTR
“recurrent lymphoma”: HL OR NHL → LNM

185 of 4,971 cancer-type values were changed by this pass — each one a trial that would otherwise have been unmatchable against its own disease.

The three layers detect different classes of error, and each of these corrections was found by only one of them.

What it produces, and what we learned

Worked example · one trial

One trial, end to end — NCT07247110

Three arms, each a different drug regimen. Two accept any solid tumour after prior therapy; the third accepts only lung cancer, in untreated patients.

Dose escalation and + Cetuximab: “locally advanced unresectable or metastatic solid tumor” · “at least 1 prior line of systemic therapy”
+ Pembrolizumab: “metastatic non-small cell lung cancer” · “must be untreated” · “has received any prior immunotherapy” (excluded)
All three: “presence of Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS) alteration” quoted verbatim from each arm's eligibility criteria

what this achieves Each arm retains its own cancer type and prior-therapy rule. Version 1 produced a single list of criteria per trial, under which a previously-treated patient would appear eligible for the pembrolizumab arm. The gene name, written out in full, resolves to two precise terms, so a KRAS point mutation and a KRAS amplification both match.
Worked example

One drug, end to end — pembrolizumab

A drug's facts are properties of the drug itself, so each is researched once and reused across every arm that administers it. 2,899 raw intervention names resolve to 1,310 distinct drugs.

Step 1 · identity

Brand and code names, resolved

“Keytruda”, “MK-3475” → pembrolizumab. The LLM supplies the name; the identifier rxcui:1547545 comes from a lookup.

Step 2 · what it is and does

Mechanism, by web search

Monoclonal antibody — target PD-1, action inhibitor. Its class codes are then attached by lookup.

Step 3 · regulatory status

TGA and PBS, per indication

Web search of official sources, per approved indication, with the date and an evidence link. This information does not appear in the protocol text.

Step 4 · role in the arm

Tested, or supporting

The same drug is the subject of one trial arm and a backbone or comparator in another. This judgement is made per arm; everything above it is shared across arms.

why this matters for matching Approval is indication-specific — so we map each drug's approved indications into the same OncoTree and finding-model vocabulary as the trial side, and the two can be compared directly.
How the mapping was developed

Mapping prompts, developed with ML methodology

Mapping free text to a controlled vocabulary is where we borrow ML discipline. Our own hand-curated resource files are the ground truth, and are held out as the test set.

The doer prompt

Grammar and worked examples

The ontology and grammar, plus a handful of positive examples taken from the curated files — what a correct mapping looks like.

The reviewer prompt

Counter-examples

Deliberately seeded with plausible-looking wrong mappings — the traps — so the reviewer learns what to reject, not only what to accept.

The process

Train, then validate

Live-test on one set, fix at the level of a rule rather than a single case, then validate on a disjoint set to guard against overfitting.

mappingtrained onheld-out validationpassed review
cancer type → OncoTree50 trials100 trials, 288 values287 / 288  (99.7%)
gene alteration → finding-model50 trials, 330 values100 trials, 242 values239 / 242  (98.8%)

The rest of each curated resource file is never shown to the mappers, so the validation set is genuinely unseen.

The result

What the matching engine receives

2,023
trials in the deliverable
5,284
trial arms
17,830
eligibility paths
1,310
distinct drugs
8
linked drug tables

One flat file for eligibility, plus a set of linked drug tables. One row = one combination of requirements a patient can satisfy for one arm of one trial, so the matching engine compares values directly.

every value stays traceable Each interpreted value keeps the quoted source text it came from and the section it was found in, so any row in the output can be taken back to the sentence that produced it.
re-runs are cheap on purpose Every LLM call is stored against a fingerprint of its exact request, so an unchanged trial costs nothing to re-process. Change a prompt and only the work that prompt affected is recomputed.
What we learned

Where it still struggles

Limit 1

The hardest trials do not converge

On deeply nested, many-cohort protocols the doer cannot satisfy every reviewer within the round budget. In our last full run, 219 of 1,999 trials (11%) ended on a best-effort answer.

Those outputs are written and marked for human review, rather than dropped.

Limit 2

Correctness costs compute

Because a reviewer may object but never edit, the doer rewrites the whole answer each round rather than patching it. This costs more tokens and more time than a targeted edit.

Limit 3

Reviewers only catch what they are asked

A mistake that no reviewer is looking for will pass. We found one such gap and closed it by adding a reviewer that reads the whole table; we cannot demonstrate that no further gap remains.

The spread

Most trials are quick

57 of the 71 finished in under five minutes. The long tail is made up of multi-cohort protocols that take several rounds with their reviewers.

Why the total is not the sum

Trials are curated concurrently

The whole set took 38 minutes rather than the four hours the individual times add up to.
